misconceptions.claim: RBAC is always the simplest and safest model.
misconceptions.correction: RBAC can be effective for stable functions, but role explosion, temporary context, and separation-of-duty requirements may call for attributes, rules, or a hybrid.

misconceptions.claim: The user interface is the enforcement point.
misconceptions.correction: APIs, services, databases, operating systems, and network boundaries must enforce independently so bypassing the UI does not bypass policy.

misconceptions.claim: A valid token remains authorized until it expires.
misconceptions.correction: High-impact systems may require fresh decisions, revocation checks, or step-up authentication when roles, device posture, or risk changes.

outcome: Given a resource and access request, select or compare an access-control model, identify policy inputs, place the decision and enforcement points, and explain how the result is reviewed or revoked.

sections.body: Discretionary access control lets an owner or creator decide access; mandatory access control applies centrally governed labels and rules; role-based access control maps permissions to job or function roles; rule-based control evaluates explicit conditions; attribute-based access control evaluates subject, object, action, and environment attributes; risk-based control adapts the decision to assessed context. The choice is not a ranking of good and bad models. It is a question of authority, information classification, change rate, auditability, and required context.
keyPoints: RBAC is useful when stable job functions map cleanly to permissions, but role explosion can become a governance problem.
ABAC and risk-based decisions can express context, but they depend on trustworthy and timely attributes.
Least privilege, need to know, and separation of duties constrain any model.
sections.title: Choose a model that matches the policy

sections.body: A policy decision point evaluates the request and returns a result; a policy enforcement point applies that result at an API, application, database, operating-system, network, or physical boundary. Centralized decisions can improve consistency while distributed enforcement preserves local control and resilience. Test both sides: a correct policy is ineffective if an enforcement path fails open, caches stale permissions, ignores a deny, trusts an unverified attribute, or cannot revoke a long-lived token.
keyPoints: A policy decision should name the subject, object, action, policy version, and relevant context.
Default deny is a prudent response when no rule authorizes a consequential action.
Fresh decisions or step-up controls may be required for high-impact actions or changed conditions.
sections.title: Separate decision from enforcement

sections.body: RBAC grants permissions through roles and supports governed job functions; rule-based access applies system-defined conditions; MAC enforces centrally controlled labels and clearances; DAC permits a resource owner to delegate within policy; ABAC evaluates subject, object, action, and environment attributes; and risk-based access changes the decision or required assurance from contextual risk. A policy decision point evaluates policy and inputs; a policy enforcement point intercepts or mediates the requested action and must fail in a policy-consistent way. Choose based on stability of job roles, classification, ownership, attribute quality, context, scale, auditability, and consequence. Failures include role explosion, untrusted attributes, policy bypass at an API, inconsistent PDP/PEP decisions, owner delegation without review, and risk signals silently converting a deny into allow.
keyPoints: Make access decisions attributable to a subject, asset, action, context, owner, policy, enforcement point, and revocation path.
Test both expected allow behavior and abuse, failure, stale-access, or unavailable-dependency behavior.
sections.title: Select, enforce, and review an authorization policy model

summary: Authorization translates policy into a permit, deny, or conditional decision for a subject attempting an action on an object. The model and enforcement architecture should express business authority, least privilege, context, and risk without relying on a successful login alone.

assumptions: The example policy requires a current care-team assignment for ordinary access.
A defined break-glass path would be a separate conditional result with its own logging and review.
Animation timing, if used by the renderer, represents presentation pacing rather than system latency.

title: Implement and manage authorization mechanisms

workedExamples.reasoning: Authentication supplies the subject, not the permit. An authorization request can combine subject role and assignment, object sensitivity and patient relationship, action, device posture, time, and emergency context. The policy may deny or require a documented break-glass path with heightened logging and review. Enforcement must apply the result at the record API, not only at the user interface.
workedExamples.situation: A clinician authenticated through SSO requests a patient's record from a managed tablet during a scheduled shift. The clinician's role permits records, but the patient is outside the clinician's assigned care team.
